labels.start_notice: A historical mission with fictional return decisions and alternate outcomes.
labels.alternate_history_explanation: The earlier return order begins the alternate-history route. The later order follows the historical timing: the original mission report (H6, p. 6-9) records western Pacific zone 3 as available on revolutions 6 and 7, with revolution 7 selected. On either route, the game's propellant warning, recovery tradeoff, crew-condition sequence, controllers' reactions, and next-mission constraints are dramatized; matching the timing does not make these consequences a reconstruction of the recovery. The post-flight stance and its relationship consequences are fictional. The historical opening — docking, the communications gap, the crew's stabilization of the spacecraft, the termination rule, and a western Pacific recovery — follows sources H1–H4. Once the earlier order activates ALTERNATE HISTORY, a later historical choice does not reset it.
labels.capcom_history_note: Houston CAPCOM for Gemini VIII was Jim Lovell. His calls in the game are dramatized from the mission's air-ground transcript (H7); the crew's quoted words are from that transcript.

notices.dramatization: Inspired by real missions and people, this game includes fictional dialogue, simplified systems, and alternate historical outcomes. These elements do not represent the actual words, beliefs, or actions of the people portrayed. NASA is not responsible for the game's interpretations, generated content, or accuracy.

sources.title: Gemini's First Docking Turns to Wild Ride in Orbit
sources.author: NASA, Bob Granath
sources.note: Supports the communication gap, crew stabilization and contingency return. It describes an orbit before historical recovery; it does not validate our two-option menu or invented extra-orbit margin. Its fault-cause wording is cautious. Used for the historical opening, not to claim simulated reserve telemetry or alternate crew conditions occurred.

sources.note: Supports ending the remaining objectives after RCS activation and the western Pacific contingency recovery. It describes a next-available-opportunity rule. sources.title: 'Tumbling End Over End': The Trauma of Gemini VIII (Part 2), March 16, 2014
sources.author: Ben Evans, AmericaSpace
sources.note: User-supplied secondary account. Its post-flight discussion supports the attributed positions summarized in the context card, including the reported exoneration. The original memoir/interview passages and timing of each criticism have not been independently verified. No direct quotes are invented; the scene is not presented as a documented meeting. H5 does not support any numerical relationship adjustment or Glen's alternate response.

sources.title: Gemini Program Mission Report, Gemini VIII (MSC-G-R-66-4), 29 April 1966
sources.author: NASA Gemini Mission Evaluation Team
sources.note: Primary NASA report, archival mirror. Read printed pp. 6-8 through 6-11 (PDF 376–379); visually checked 6-9. Describes zone 3 availability on revolutions 6 and 7, the choice of revolution 7, termination conditions, and real-time versus postflight RCS estimates. Does not establish the game risk tradeoff or six outcomes. Original nasa.gov file URL returned 404 on 2026-09-07.

sources.title: Gemini VIII voice communications: air-to-ground, ground-to-air and onboard transcription
sources.author: NASA-hosted mission transcript
sources.note: Read PDF pp. 75–79; visually checked PDF 77 (printed 76). Used for short calls, readbacks, uncertain reports and crew autonomy, not as dialogue to reproduce. Onboard/air-ground speech is not a complete Houston flight-loop transcript; noisy OCR was checked against the scan. No numeric propellant readings copied into the game. Content 0.5.3: visually checked PDF pp. 72, 76–79 (printed 71, 75–78). Docking 06:33:52; emergency 07:17:15 (P, Scott); regaining control 07:20:05/07:21:12; Hawaii return/control discussion 07:38:07–07:39:53. Each CAPCOM line has page-specific provenance or a procedural tag. Houston relay framing is dramatized.

fiction.title: Contact rehearsal
fiction.text: Supplemental sender/acknowledgement exercise, readback document and its later ground handoff effects. These are performed fictional rehearsals, not astronaut training prerequisites.

fiction.title: Recovery rehearsal
fiction.text: Supplemental pickup ownership/readback exercise and the fictional rework it can avoid. Preparation does not move recovery forces closer.

fiction.title: Systems rehearsal
fiction.text: Supplemental warning-routing exercise, its readback and its operational handoff effects. Preparation does not add control reserve or identify the hardware fault.

fiction.title: Air-support and surface-retrieval reports
fiction.text: Original abstract status reports, now supporting a real operational choice. No claim to historical ship/aircraft positions.

fiction.title: Recovery coordination events
fiction.text: The fictional ground ownership clarification, acknowledgement retry and pickup approach consequences. These are explicitly events of the game room, not errors by historical astronauts or operators.

fiction.title: Procedure adoption
fiction.text: Two original standing-procedure choices and their reference pages. Neither reverses the operational outcome or the next-mission rehearsal constraint.

fiction.title: Alternate return envelope and outcomes
fiction.text: Both selectable opportunities, extra modeled orbit, ordinal critical-reserve warning, earlier sea wait, concentrated later pickup, all six execution/consequence cases, all crew-condition variations, and the six outcome titles. Both routes are authored to be viable in this simplified scenario and both end with the crew alive. There are no numerical chances or hidden survival roll. Actual orbital feasibility, exact fuel quantities, precise recovery time and medical diagnoses are not asserted. Neither branch is labeled the exact historical result. All figures who execute onboard operations remain competent. H6 confirms a historical choice of return revolution; the fictional element is this menu’s specific operational tradeoff and outcomes, not the existence of a timing decision.

fiction.title: Named fictional controllers and operational relationships
fiction.text: Mara Voss and Elias Reed, their recommendations, recovery responses, trust-point changes and notes. These are original characters reusing the SYSTEMS and RECOVERY portrait slots. Negative trust never suppresses safety information. The separate user-authorized astronaut relationship branch is F10.

fiction.title: Gemini IX-A planning constraints
fiction.text: Compulsory recovery or systems rehearsal following the experienced return risk; the three offered two-exercise plans; branch eligibility; and the player's persisted plan commitment. These are operational preparation consequences in the fictional campaign, not the historical IX-A roster, schedule or training program.

fiction.title: Post-flight stance and social consequences
fiction.text: Glen's two statements; the compressed later discussion scene; blaming the crew versus accepting ground contingency responsibility; Armstrong/Scott trust -2 each and Cunningham/Stafford +1 each plus a deepened corps rift on the blame route; Armstrong/Scott +1 each and critics unchanged on the ground route; all associated narration, facts, notes and IX-A relationship displays; and the concrete commissioned docked-contingency task. These are fictional consequences of the player's choice. The ground-side criticism itself is sourced through H5, but its exact implementation and resulting relationship gains are not asserted as historical events. Choosing to blame the crew does not change their demonstrated actions or the source's reported exoneration. Choosing ground responsibility does not erase the existence of disagreement.

fiction.title: Illustrated prologue and recovery presentation
fiction.text: Original staged illustrations, lighting, weather, visual motion, the overview-to-preparation transition, recovery tier labels and result-line summaries. The six underlying game outcomes remain the simplified model described in F7. Different plate lighting expresses tone, not a measured recovery time, storm, medical finding or new consequence. Portrait expressions represent the game relationship changes in F8 and F10; they do not document the real astronauts’ feelings or add their words.

Take the flight director’s seat in a story-driven mission control game. Play the Gemini VIII demo. An independent tribute to the people of the space program.

Failure is Not an Option — home
FAILURE IS NOT AN OPTION A FLIGHT DIRECTOR GAME
Two astronauts. A damaged spacecraft. The next call is yours.
Gemini VIII · Play in your browser
History sets the scene. Your decisions shape what follows.
Take the flight director’s seat in a narrative game inspired by real missions and the people who made them possible.

You are Glen Kurtz: a fictional tribute to the legendary Gene Kranz, whose leadership helped guide Mission Control through pivotal moments of Gemini and Apollo. The signature vest is a nod to Kranz; Glen’s story is his own. Ageless by design, he represents generations of flight directors, from the earliest missions to those still ahead.

Listen to your controllers. Weigh incomplete information. Make the call, then live with its consequences. Follow the historical path or branch into an alternate outcome. The astronauts are real; the decisions and consequences blend documented events with clearly identified fiction.
Your controllers see different risks. Ask questions and work through the evidence before you commit.
Getting the crew home means weighing time in orbit against the conditions awaiting them at sea.
Your preparations and orders affect the return. Your response afterward shapes relationships and the next planning step.
GEMINI VIII The Weight of the Call
A historic docking. A sudden emergency. Armstrong and Scott have brought their spacecraft back under control. Now your team must bring them home.
Prepare your controllers, weigh competing return risks, and face the consequences of your decision in the post-flight discussion.

A lifelong dream. A new trajectory.
I’m Dan Lee-Odinson, a Technical Project Manager and Space Studies student at Everglades University.

My fascination with space began when I was six, holding my breath as Discovery’s STS-26 crew launched on the historic Return to Flight after the Challenger disaster. Watching Artemis II lift off in April 2026 turned that lifelong passion into a determination to be part of what comes next.
Since then, I’ve been working toward one goal: to learn everything I can and bring my skills to a future career in Mission Operations and Program Management.

I’m inspired by the people of NASA and the space agencies and companies around the world expanding what humanity can do in space—and by the dedication of everyone on the ground who makes those journeys possible.
This game is my tribute to you all.
